title: Canada's First Spacewalk in Seven Years Will Add Station Power
summary: On Thursday, October 29, at 8 a.m. ET, Canada's Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Anil Menon are scheduled to step outside the International Space Station for a spacewalk. It will be the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in seven years, and Kutryk's first ever. Menon has done three spacewalks before. The walk should last about 6 hours and 45 minutes. Their job is to put up new solar panels, called iROSAs, to give the station more power. This is the first of two spacewalks; the second will come no sooner than November 5. They will raise power from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts, a boost of roughly 30 percent. Canadarm2, the station's robotic arm, will help move an array into place, while NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins move the arm. Kutryk will climb hand-over-hand to the site, and the pair will bolt the array on and let it unfold from about 10 feet to around 20 feet. Garrett Hehn compared the arrays to a snap bracelet. Jenni Gibbons will be the capsule communicator for the spacewalks.
why_it_matters: It shows you how sunlight can be turned into power, just like the solar panels that can power lights and devices here on Earth.

keywords.explanation: A spacewalk is when an astronaut steps outside a spacecraft to do work in space.
iROSAs are new solar panels that are put up outside the space station to make more power.
Kilowatts are units that tell how much electric power something makes or uses.
Canadarm2 is the space station's long robotic arm that moves big parts into place.
A capsule communicator is the person on the ground who talks to the astronauts during a spacewalk.

background_read: The International Space Station is a large home and laboratory that orbits Earth, where astronauts live and work.
Solar panels catch sunlight and turn it into power for the station's lights, tools, and machines.
On a spacewalk, astronauts put on special suits and step outside the station to build or fix things.
